To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a fusion protein formed by lateral transfer of genes from a cyanobacterium to an ancestor of the dinoflagells was targeted to the plastid and that the O-methyltransferse moiety of the protein remained plastid targeted when it separated from the shikimate pathway protein.
a multigene unit from a cyanobacterium was cotransferred to dinoflagelates and resulted in a fusion protein that targeted the plastid.

(i) lateral transfer of a gene region from a cyanobacterium to an ancestor of the dinoflagelates occurred before the divergence of Oxyrrhis and Perkinsus; (ii) the transferred region included a paralogue (AroB) of a shikimate biosynthesis enzyme and an O-methylation transferase (OMT); (iii) the AroB and OMT proteins were fused together to form a novel plastid-localized fusion protein;
In summary, our research is concerned with

lateral gene transfer and its biological implications and provides a case study of a well-defined transfer from a cyanophyte donor to a dinoflagellae recipient that resulted in a novel fusion protein that was targeted to the dinophyte plastid.
lateral gene transfer and the evolution of gene fusions and their reversion.
a well-characterized example of lateral gene transfer, the biological implications of which are discussed in the context of a novel plastid fusion protein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the transfer of the AroB/OMT fusion from a cyanobacterium into an ancestor of dinodinoflagellates occurred before Oxyrrhisis but after Perkinsus, and the transfer was followed by a reversion to 2 individual plastid-localized proteins in Karlodinium, with the OMT protein acquiring a new plastid-targeting signal.
this is a case of gene fusion followed by reversion to 2 individual proteins in the same organism.
the transfer occurred from cyanobacteria, the fusion occurred before the Perkinsus-Oxyrrhis divergence, and the fusion reverted in Karlodinium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lateral gene transfer can occur between distantly related eukaryotic species but that the fate of the transferred gene depends on the function of the protein.

the fusion of AroB and OMT occurred in a common ancestor of Perkinsus and Oxyrrhis and that the OMT was subsequently targeted to and maintained in the plastid in Oxyrrhis, but that in Karlodinium the OMT separated from Aro B and acquired its own plastid targeting peptide.

the transfer of a gene fusion from a cyanobacterium to a dinoflagellated ancestor resulted in a novel fusion protein that was targeted to the plastid and that subsequently reverted to 1 of the original genes in a subset of the dinoflagelates, which retained plastid localization for the OMT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gene transfer can be a very powerful tool for the evolution of novel functions, and the evolution of plastid-targeting sequences can be very dynamic.
gene fusion events are not as rare as previously thought, and the transfer of genes between cyanobacteria and dinoflagellales is more common than previously thought.

lateral gene transfer is a powerful force in the evolutionary development of eukaryotes and that it can be a major force in the development of novel functions in the plastid, the most important and widespread organelle in eukaryotes.
